title: Global and Local Inversions
statement:
The array `nums` of length `n` holds each integer from `0` to `n - 1` exactly once.

- A **global inversion** is a pair of indices `(i, j)` with `0 <= i < j < n` and `nums[i] > nums[j]`.
- A **local inversion** is an index `i` with `0 <= i < n - 1` and `nums[i] > nums[i + 1]`.

Return `true` when `nums` has exactly as many global inversions as local inversions, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: All values in nums are distinct
nums is a permutation of 0 to n - 1
notes:
## Intuition

Every local inversion is also a global one, so the two counts are equal exactly when there is no inversion between positions at least two apart. Counting both directly is O(n²) (the brute force), but a permutation allows a closed-form test: the counts match exactly when every value sits at most one place from its own index, `|nums[i] - i| <= 1`.

- If `nums[i] >= i + 2`, the `nums[i]` smaller values cannot all fit in the `i` places before `i`, so at least two of them lie after `i`, one at least two places away: a non-local inversion.
- If `nums[i] <= i - 2`, the same counting with larger values puts one of them at least two places before `i`.
- If every value is within one of its index, then for `j >= i + 2`, `nums[i] <= i + 1 <= j - 1 <= nums[j]`, so no distant pair is inverted.

## Approach

1. For each index `i`, compute `gap = |nums[i] - i|`.
2. If `gap > 1`, a distant inversion exists: return `false`.
3. If no index fails, return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 0, 2]`: at `i = 0`, `gap = |1 - 0| = 1`; at `i = 1`, `gap = |0 - 1| = 1`; at `i = 2`, `gap = 0`. No gap exceeds 1, so the answer is `true` (one global inversion, which is also the one local inversion).

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the array.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Counting all inversions with two nested loops is O(n²) and too slow for `n = 10^5`.
- Checking only `nums[i] > nums[i + 2]` is not enough: in `[2, 0, 3, 1]` the only distant inversion is between indices 0 and 3.
- The gap rule relies on `nums` being a permutation of `0..n-1`; it does not hold for arbitrary arrays.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `i` | the index being checked |
| `gap` | how far the value `nums[i]` sits from its own index `i` |

narration.2: n is the length of the permutation.
narration.3: Visit every index of the permutation.
narration.4: gap measures how far the value at i sits from its own index.
narration.5: A value two or more places from its own index forces an inversion between distant positions.
narration.6: Such an inversion is global but not local, so the counts differ.
narration.9: Every value is within one place of its index, so every inversion is between neighbours and the counts are equal.
